query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Training a data-driven interatomic potential (e.g., a neural network or Gaussian process) on diverse ab initio configurations specifically targeting the high-temperature liquid regime will yield significantly better phase-space overlap with ab initio calculations and reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatches compared to standard EAM references in multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their melting points.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys in both solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures (up to ~20% above Tm).
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy a machine-learned interatomic potential fitted against ab initio snapshots, ensuring coverage of the broad configurational space in the liquid (including near-critical fluctuations) and near-melting solid phases.
generation.conditions: Alloy compositions featuring two or more principal elements, with ab initio reference data sets curated at multiple temperatures above 0.8 Tm and up to ~1.2 Tm to capture relevant solid–liquid transition regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: A flexible potential form (e.g., neural network) that accurately replicates key short-range and medium-range order in the high-temperature liquid and transition states.
generation.mechanism: By encompassing adequately sampled ab initio liquid-state configurations, the machine-learned potential will account for complex local bonding and disorder, enabling more faithful representation of the free-energy landscape and thus improving thermodynamic integration accuracy relative to EAM.
generation.predicted_outcome: Approximately a 10–30% decrease in free-energy integration path mismatches compared with EAM-based references in TOR-TILD calculations for near-melting solids and liquids.
generation.baseline: Standard EAM reference potentials in TOR-TILD comparisons, which exhibit limited configurational fidelity in the disordered high-temperature regime.
generation.boundary: Applies where representative ab initio liquid and near-melting data can be generated for the targeted multicomponent alloys; less certain if extrapolated significantly beyond the training domain or for systems with large chemical or structural inhomogeneity.
generation.uncertainty: Actual accuracy gain depends on the quality and breadth of ab initio training data and may vary across different compositions and temperatures. Additional tuning of the ML architecture may be needed for new compositional spaces.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform direct ab initio thermodynamic integration on representative solid–liquid systems for a range of multicomponent alloys at temperatures near and above their melting points. Compare free-energy predictions from the trained ML potential versus both ab initio calculations (ground truth) and standard EAM-based TOR-TILD results to quantify discrepancies.
measurements: Root-mean-square deviations in energy and forces
Structural metrics (e.g., radial distribution functions) in liquid and near-melting regimes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the new ML-based reference potential fails to reduce free-energy mismatches by the predicted 10–30% compared to EAM references, or if it does not reliably capture the liquid-phase structural features validated by ab initio calculations, the hypothesis is falsified.

The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both the liquid and A2 phases were established. By applying these expressions, the thermodynamic properties down to 0 K and thermal vacancy near the melting point can be well described. Besides, the lattice stability of Cr and V over the whole temperature range can be guaranteed. Based on the third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure elements, the Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were thermodynamically assessed by considering the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD approach. A strategy to estimate the Gibbs energy of Laves phase was proposed by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as semiempirical relation. Such a method was applied to C14 and C15 Laves phases in Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems. The calculated phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties showed nice agreement with the measured ones. Significant improvements can be observed at low temperatures compared with those from the second-generation thermodynamic descriptions, indicating the high reliability of the present thermodynamic descriptions.

decision.trend: Early atomistic modeling of high-entropy alloys primarily employed classical EAM-type potentials to describe both solid and near-melting liquid states. While such references can capture some aspects of crystallographic stability and mechanical properties at lower temperatures, their limited functional forms have proven inadequate for modeling the large configuration space of high-temperature liquids. Over time, researchers shifted toward first-principles methods and high-throughput density-functional theory to probe multicomponent alloy phase stability and transformations, but these approaches are too expensive for routine simulations of molten phases. The 2024 study on melting simulations of high-entropy carbonitrides using a deep-learning potential (PMC11576752::webcard) demonstrated that machine-learned force fields can reproduce ab initio–quality accuracy at high temperatures and in disordered states, signaling a transition from strictly classical EAM references toward more flexible and systematically improvable potential forms.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress with advanced machine-learning potentials for particular compositions (e.g., (TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25), there is not yet a standardized workflow to build, validate, and apply these references for a wide range of multicomponent high-entropy alloys in both solid and liquid states at high temperatures. The degree to which these new potentials solve the longstanding reference–target phase-space overlap problem—and how broadly they achieve quantitative accuracy for free energies and thermodynamic integration—remains to be definitively established.
decision.lever: Train a neural network or Gaussian process potential on ab initio snapshots specifically targeting diverse high-temperature liquid and near-melting configurations across a representative set of multicomponent alloys (including the precise composition region of concern). Systematically refine sampling of ab initio data to ensure coverage of liquid-phase disorder and interfacial transitions. Validate the reference potential via direct free-energy calculations from thermodynamic integration and compare with new ab initio thermodynamic paths.
decision.why: Machine-learned interatomic potentials provide the flexibility needed to capture the configurational complexity of high-entropy alloy liquids, addressing the poor phase-space overlap that occurs with EAM references. By systematically expanding the training data to include high-temperature liquid structures, the new potential can reduce mismatches in thermodynamic-integration paths relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM-based references. Elemental and binary ML-based simulations have already demonstrated superior accuracy in capturing liquid thermodynamics. A decisive free-energy benchmark can be performed by comparing computed Helmholtz free energies from the new ML-based reference potential with direct ab initio thermodynamic integration results for selected compositions (e.g., multi-principal alloys that vary systematically in atomic ratio), across a relevant temperature range near and above their melting points; any substantial discrepancy would falsify the hypothesis that the improved potential accurately spans the target phase space.
